h1: The 8 Best Laptop Locks Under $150 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Laptop Locks Under $150: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 laptop cable locks scored on slot fit, cable length and resettable codes, from Kensington universal locks to MacBook options.
summary: The Kensington Universal 3-in-1 is the lock to buy if you own more than one laptop or may switch, since one cable fits standard, nano and wedge-style slots. The Multplx Universal is the alternative that also covers MacBooks, and the I3C adds an anchor plate for laptops with no slot. Every lock here costs well under $150, so fit, not price, decides the winner.
intro: A $150 ceiling is generous for a laptop lock, and the evidence is in the lineup: every model we ranked costs under $50. So spending is not the decision. The decision is whether the lock head physically fits your laptop, because a modern thin-and-light often has a nano slot, an old workhorse has a wide one, and a MacBook has no slot at all.

That makes compatibility the first score, followed by cable length, code security and how easy it is to reset. We reviewed eight cable locks and ranked them on those points. One honest note up front: a cable lock slows a thief down, it does not defeat one, because a determined person with bolt cutters or a pry bar can still beat the cable or the laptop chassis.

products.name: Kensington Universal 3-in-1 Combination Laptop Lock
products.verdict: One lock head for standard and nano slots, with a 6-foot cut-resistant cable.
products.description:
Kensington's Universal 3-in-1 is the only lock here sold as working in more than one slot type: it fits standard and nano slots from a single head. That matters because laptops change faster than locks, and a universal head follows you from an old work machine to a new thin one.

It wins because the others each cover one slot family. The 1.8 m (6 ft) carbon steel cable has a plastic sheath that resists cutting, and the four-number dial resets to your choice of code. Against the two Kensington single-slot locks, it costs a little more and gives up nothing but a slightly bulkier head.

Buy it for a household or office with mixed laptops. The caveat is that universal heads fit slots, not slotless designs, so a MacBook still needs a different approach.
pros: Fits more than one slot type
cons: Head is bulkier than slim locks
products.idealFor: Mixed fleets of laptops or buyers who upgrade often.
products.skipIf: Your laptop has no security slot at all.

products.name: Multplx Universal Laptop Security Lock
products.verdict: A universal lock that names MacBooks, Surface and Dell as supported.
products.description:
Multplx sells a universal laptop security lock and states it works with MacBooks, Surface and Dell machines. The cable is described as extremely durable and cut-resistant steel meant to tether the laptop to a desk.

It ranks just below the Kensington Universal because the Kensington documents its slot types, cable length and code range, while the Multplx listing is more general. Its advantage is the explicit mention of MacBook and Surface, two families that frustrate buyers of slot-only locks. For those users it is the more reassuring listing.

Pick it if your laptop is a MacBook or Surface and you want a single lock. The caveat is that the listing gives no cable length or code details, so check the product page before relying on it for a long tether.
products.idealFor: MacBook and Surface owners wanting one lock.
products.skipIf: You want full documentation of length and code.

products.name: I3C Laptop Cable Lock
products.verdict: Includes an anchor plate so MacBooks and slotless laptops can be locked.
products.description:
I3C solves the slotless problem with an anchor plate for MacBooks, plus a standard lock head for most other laptops. The lock head itself is stainless steel, which resists wear better than painted zinc.

It ranks third because the plate approach is a workaround, not a real security slot. The Kensington Universal gives a stronger connection into a laptop's reinforced slot, while the I3C relies on an adhesive plate, so its protection depends on how well that plate bonds. For a MacBook, it is still better than nothing, and it has more clarity than a generic listing.

Best for slotless laptops where the choice is a plate or no lock at all. The caveat is that adhesive plates can mar a finish when removed, so decide before you stick it.
cons: Plate is weaker than a slot
products.idealFor: MacBook owners and anyone with a slotless laptop.
products.skipIf: Your laptop has a real security slot.

products.name: Kensington Combination Laptop Lock for Standard Security Slot
products.verdict: A slim-head standard-slot lock with a 5-foot cable for under $25.
products.description:
This Kensington is built for the standard security slot and uses a slim lock head so it fits thin laptops without crowding adjacent ports. The 5-foot (1.5 m) carbon steel cable resists cutting, and the four-wheel code is yours to reset.

It ranks fourth because it covers only one slot type, which the 3-in-1 outdoes for slightly more money. Against its sibling nano-slot lock, it is simply the other half of the pair: pick the one that matches the slot on your laptop. At under $25 it is the cheapest of the Kensington locks here.

Buy it if you know your slot is standard and you want the lowest price from a brand whose hardware is widely supported. The caveat is a 5-foot cable, a foot shorter than the 6-foot models.
products.idealFor: Confirmed standard-slot laptops on a budget.
products.skipIf: Your laptop uses a nano slot.

products.name: Kensington Combination Laptop Lock for Nano Size Security Slot
products.verdict: The nano-slot version of the slim Kensington, with the same 5-foot cable.
products.description:
Thin modern ultrabooks use a nano-size security slot, and this Kensington is cut to fit it. It keeps the 5-foot (1.5 m) carbon steel cable, the slim lock head and the resettable four-wheel code of its standard-slot twin.

It ranks fifth because the Universal 3-in-1 also handles nano slots and adds length, though at a higher price. If you are certain your laptop is nano-only, this model gets you the same security for under $25. The risk is buying the wrong one, since a standard head will not seat in a nano slot.

Pick it for an ultrabook owner who wants the least expensive branded lock. The caveat is cable length: five feet limits where you can anchor.
products.idealFor: Ultrabook owners confident their slot is nano.
products.skipIf: You are unsure which slot type you have.

products.name: Kensington Combination Cable T-Bar Standard Lock Slot for Laptops
products.verdict: A T-bar standard lock with 10,000 combinations and a 6-foot cable.
products.description:
This Kensington uses a T-bar locking mechanism for standard slots and is listed for HP, Lenovo and Acer laptops. It has a resettable four-wheel code with 10,000 possible combinations and a 6-foot carbon steel cable that is cut-resistant and anchors to desks.

It ranks sixth because the T-bar design is an older style compared with the newer slim heads, and it fits standard slots only. The extra foot of cable over the 5-foot models is useful for wrapping around a heavy desk leg. Against the N17 Dell model, it fits a wider range of brands.

Good for office laptops that need a long tether. The caveat is the head size, which can crowd the side of a thin machine.
products.idealFor: Office HP, Lenovo and Acer laptops.
products.skipIf: Your laptop is very thin or uses a nano slot.

products.name: Kensington N17 Dell Laptop Computer Lock
products.verdict: A Dell-specific lock with a unique engagement and 10,000 combinations.
products.description:
The N17 is made to fit Dell laptops, with a head designed to seat seamlessly in their security slot. It has a resettable four-wheel code with 10,000 possible combinations, and a unique engagement that forms a strong connection to the machine.

It ranks seventh because it is brand-specific, and the Universal 3-in-1 does the same job for Dell and others at the same price bucket. Where the N17 helps is on older Dell laptops with the Dell-style slot, where a generic head can fit loosely. For those users it is the safest match.

Buy it only for Dell machines that match. The caveat is limited flexibility: if you change brands, the lock becomes less useful.
products.idealFor: Older Dell laptops with the matching slot.
products.skipIf: You may switch brands or own multiple makes.

products.name: Kensington NanoSaver Combination Laptop Lock
products.verdict: A 6-foot combination lock for select HP laptops with a four-wheel code.
products.description:
The NanoSaver is listed for select HP laptops, with a resettable four-wheel number code and a 6-foot carbon steel cable in a plastic sheath that resists cutting. The sheath protects desk finishes from the cable.

It ranks last because the compatibility is narrow and the listing says select models, which means you must verify your laptop. The Universal 3-in-1 offers the same 6-foot cable and more fit options for a similar price. The NanoSaver only wins if your HP model is on its list.

Buy it after checking the HP model list on the product page. The caveat is that a wrong match wastes the purchase, since nano heads are not interchangeable with standard ones.
products.skipIf: Your laptop is not on the compatibility list.

whatMatters.detail: Laptops use a standard slot, a thinner nano slot, or none at all. The head must match, or it will not seat. Check the side of your laptop for the small lock symbol and measure the slot. The Kensington Universal 3-in-1 fits standard and nano, while single-slot Kensingtons do not cross over.

Length decides what you can anchor to. Five feet reaches a table leg, six feet wraps a heavy desk base. Kensington's T-bar, NanoSaver and Universal use 6 feet, and the single-slot locks use 5 feet. Check the listing for the stated length, and measure your anchor point first.

A four-wheel code has up to 10,000 combinations, which stops casual tampering but not a patient attacker. Kensington's T-bar and N17 list 10,000. Pick a code that is not your birth year, and verify that it can be reset. A resettable code means you never need to ship the lock back.

Carbon steel cables resist common snips better than plain wire, and a plastic sheath adds scratch protection. Even so, bolt cutters defeat any cable lock. Treat the cable as a deterrent. Look for named steel and a sheath, and anchor to something fixed, like a bolted desk or pillar.

MacBooks and some thin machines have no security slot. Adhesive anchor plates, like the I3C, add one, but they are only as strong as their bond. The Multplx claims MacBook support, so read how it attaches. If your laptop is slotless, consider whether a lock is the right security tool at all.

faq.q: How do I know which slot my laptop has?
faq.a: Look for a small lock icon on the side or back. A standard slot is wider, a nano slot is thin. If you are unsure, the Kensington Universal 3-in-1 fits both, which avoids a wrong purchase.

faq.q: Will a MacBook accept these locks?
faq.a: Most MacBooks have no security slot. The I3C Laptop Cable Lock includes an anchor plate, and the Multplx lists MacBook support. Standard Kensington locks will not attach without a plate or adapter.

faq.q: Is the Universal 3-in-1 worth it over the single-slot Kensingtons?
faq.a: If you may change laptops, yes. It handles standard and nano slots with a 6-foot cable. If you know your slot, the 5-foot standard or nano model saves a few dollars.

faq.q: How do I set the code?
faq.a: Follow the reset instructions in the box, usually by moving a switch and dialing a new combination. The T-bar and N17 offer 10,000 combinations, so avoid obvious numbers like 0000 or 1234.

faq.q: Can a thief cut the cable?
faq.a: With bolt cutters, yes. A carbon steel cable and sheath deter casual theft, not determined attackers. Anchor to a fixed object, and pair the lock with software tracking for valuable laptops.

faq.q: Does the lock damage the slot?
faq.a: Not if used correctly. Do not yank the laptop against the cable, since the slot is a small reinforced point. Slim heads like the Kensington Standard and Nano put less leverage on thin chassis.

finalTake: Most buyers should take the Kensington Universal 3-in-1, because it fits standard and nano slots and brings a 6-foot cable. The Multplx and I3C are the options for MacBooks and slotless machines. Use the single-slot Kensingtons only when you are sure of your slot, and remember that no cable lock stops a determined thief.
